body:
How long does a patent last?

Section 53 of the Patents Act, 1970, establishes a normal term of 20 years from the date of filing the patent application. For an international application filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty designating India, the term is calculated from the relevant international filing date.

The date of grant is important because it marks the grant of enforceable patent protection, but it does not begin a fresh 20-year period. If examination and grant take several years, those years form part of the overall term measured from filing.

Patent protection is also subject to payment of the prescribed renewal fees. Failure to pay within the legally permitted period may cause the patent to cease to have effect before the end of its normal term.

What rights does a granted patent provide?

Section 48 specifies the exclusive rights of patentees. The rights depend on whether the patented subject matter is a product or a process.

Type of patentUnauthorised acts the patentee may prevent in India
Product patentMaking, using, offering for sale or selling the patented product, or importing it for those purposes
Process patentUsing the patented process, and using, offering for sale or selling the product obtained directly by that process, or importing that product for those purposes

A product patent is directed to the claimed product itself. A process patent is directed to the claimed method and includes the statutory rights concerning products obtained directly by that process.

For example, if a valid patent protects a particular manufactured device, a competitor's unauthorised manufacture of a device falling within the granted claims may infringe the patent. If a patent protects a manufacturing process, unauthorised use of that process may infringe even where the final product resembles a product obtainable by other methods.

What is patent infringement?

Patent infringement occurs when a person carries out an act covered by the enforceable patent rights without the patent holder's consent and without a legally applicable exception or defence.

Determining infringement requires identifying the granted claims, interpreting their scope and examining the accused product or process. It is not enough to say that 2 products look similar or serve the same purpose.

An inventor who independently develops a technology may still infringe an earlier valid patent if the later product or process falls within the earlier patent's enforceable claims. Independent development does not automatically remove the patent holder's statutory rights.

Simple infringement distinction

Suppose a valid patent covers a specified technical mechanism in a water-control device. Another manufacturer makes and sells a device containing all the relevant features covered by an enforceable claim, without permission. This may amount to infringement. Merely selling a different device that achieves water conservation through a mechanism outside the patent's enforceable claims does not establish infringement of that claim simply because both devices save water.

Important exceptions and limitations

Patent rights are not unlimited. The Act recognises circumstances in which specified acts do not amount to unlawful exploitation of a patent.

Research and teaching

Section 47 permits specified uses of patented inventions merely for experiment or research, including imparting instruction to pupils. This provision should not be confused with unlimited permission for ordinary commercial manufacture.

Regulatory approval activities

Section 107A permits making, constructing, using, selling or importing a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information required under laws in India or another country regulating the manufacture, construction, use, sale or import of products. This is commonly associated with the Bolar exception, which can assist preparation for regulatory approval. The exception is subject to its statutory conditions.

Government use

Section 47 permits making or importing patented articles or articles made by a patented process, and using patented processes, by or on behalf of the Government merely for its own use. These provisions do not amount to a general waiver of every patent right.

What happens if a patent is infringed?

A patentee may seek relief through the courts. Under Sections 104 and 108, patent infringement suits cannot be instituted in a court below a district court having jurisdiction, and available remedies include an injunction and, where appropriate, damages or an account of profits.

An injunction is an order restricting unlawful conduct. Damages compensate for legally recognised loss, while an account of profits addresses profits attributable to infringement. The precise remedy depends on the court's determination and the applicable law.

Compulsory licensing: a public-interest limitation

A patent holder ordinarily controls whether to license the invention. However, Indian patent law also provides for compulsory licensing in specified circumstances.

Under Section 84, an interested person may apply to the Controller for a compulsory licence after 3 years from the grant of the patent on grounds including unmet reasonable public requirements, lack of availability at a reasonably affordable price or failure to work the invention in India.

The licence is not automatic after 3 years. The Controller must consider the statutory grounds and relevant conditions before deciding whether to grant it. Ordinarily, the applicant must first try unsuccessfully to obtain a voluntary licence on reasonable terms; exceptions include national emergency, extreme urgency, public non-commercial use and established anti-competitive practices.

What happens after expiry?

Once the patent expires, the exclusive rights under that patent end. The subject matter is no longer protected by that particular patent. However, a person using the technology must still consider other independent patents and applicable legal requirements.

Prelims focus

  • Section 48 defines the exclusive rights of patentees.
  • Section 53 sets the normal patent term at 20 years from filing.
  • A PCT application designating India uses the relevant international filing date for calculating the term.
  • Section 47 includes an exception for specified experimental, research and teaching uses.
  • Section 107A addresses specified regulatory approval activities.
  • Under Section 84, a compulsory licence may be sought after 3 years from grant on specified grounds.
  • Trap: The 20-year term runs from filing; the ordinary Section 84 compulsory-licence waiting period runs from grant.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 47, 48, 53, 84, 104, 107A and 108, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); Intellectual Property India, Basics of Patents, sections on patent rights and duration (consulted 14 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: The 20-year patent term starts at filing; enforceable rights are granted later. Unpaid renewal fees may cause early cessation. PCT uses international filing.
pictures.caption: The normal 20-year term is measured from filing, not from grant.

title: Patent Term, Infringement and Exceptions to Exclusive Rights

body:
From a technical idea to a patent application

Patent fundamentals become easier to understand when applied to a realistic invention. Consider a hypothetical startup in Gujarat that develops a new mechanism to reduce leakage from water-distribution equipment.

The startup has built a working prototype and believes its mechanism performs better than existing products. Successful operation is useful evidence of practical application, but it does not automatically establish that the mechanism is new or inventive.

Step 1: identify the actual invention

The startup should distinguish the general aim of reducing water wastage from the specific technical mechanism it has developed. Patent protection concerns the claimed technical product or process, not the general social objective.

If the mechanism is simply an arrangement of known devices that continue to work independently in their usual ways, Section 3(f) may present a problem. If it produces a genuine technical result through a non-obvious arrangement, it may potentially qualify, subject to the complete patentability assessment.

Step 2: investigate earlier knowledge

The startup should search earlier patents, technical publications and other relevant public information. A patent search helps identify whether the proposed invention has already been disclosed and which features may distinguish it from earlier technology.

Finding no identical patent in an initial search does not guarantee novelty or freedom to manufacture. Relevant prior art may exist elsewhere, and another patent may cover a broader technical feature incorporated in the new product.

Step 3: assess patentability

The invention must pass the positive statutory tests and the exclusions:

  • Novelty: the claimed mechanism must not already be anticipated by qualifying prior art.
  • Inventive step: the difference must satisfy the statutory technical-advance or economic-significance requirement and be non-obvious to a skilled person.
  • Industrial applicability: the mechanism must be capable of being made or used in industry.
  • Eligibility: the claim must not fall within an exclusion under Section 3 or Section 4.

Step 4: prepare the application and complete the procedure

An eligible applicant may file a complete specification or begin with a provisional specification and subsequently submit a complete specification within the statutory 12-month period. The complete specification must explain the invention and contain claims defining the requested protection.

Ordinary publication occurs after 18 months from the filing date or priority date, whichever is earlier, subject to applicable exceptions and early-publication provisions. Examination requires a separate request. A patent is granted only if the application meets the statutory requirements and the applicable procedure has been completed.

Gujarat's Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre

Gujarat has a dedicated institutional mechanism to help innovators understand and use intellectual property protection. The Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre (IPFC), formerly known as the Patent Information Centre, operates under the Gujarat Council on Science and Technology (GUJCOST), Department of Science and Technology, Government of Gujarat, at Gandhinagar.

According to its official description, IPFC was established in collaboration with the Department of Science and Technology, Government of India. It supports students, researchers, startups, micro, small and medium enterprises, academic institutions and other innovators.

Its patent-related services include intellectual property awareness, patent searches, documentation guidance and assistance with filing procedures. The centre also provides broader intellectual property facilitation services.

Facilitation is not grant

GUJCOST's IPFC assists innovators; the Indian Patent Office administers patent examination and grant. Receiving guidance or filing assistance from a state-level institution does not mean that a patent has been granted.

After grant: using the protected invention

If the hypothetical startup receives a valid patent, its enforceable rights depend on the granted claims. It may use the invention itself or permit another enterprise to use it through a lawful licence. A licence gives permission according to agreed terms; it does not itself establish that the underlying patent is valid or that unrelated regulatory approvals are unnecessary.

The patent remains subject to statutory limitations and renewal requirements. Its normal term is 20 years from filing rather than from the date the startup first sells the product or receives the patent grant.

One-glance revision of patent fundamentals

The central concepts form a connected sequence. First, identify a specific technical product or process. Second, examine novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and statutory exclusions. Third, disclose the invention through the required specification, with claims defining the requested scope. Fourth, follow filing, publication, examination and any opposition proceedings. Finally, distinguish the grant of rights from their duration, infringement and legal exceptions.

Prelims focus

  • Novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability and statutory eligibility are cumulative patentability requirements.
  • A complete specification must contain claims defining the requested scope of protection.
  • Filing, publication, examination and grant are different stages.
  • Patent opposition concerns patentability or validity; infringement concerns unauthorised acts covered by enforceable claims.
  • GUJCOST's IPFC is located in Gandhinagar and provides patent-related facilitation services.
  • Trap: A patent search or filing-assistance service is not a patent-granting authority.

[Sources: Government of India, The Patents Act, 1970, Sections 2(1)(j), 3, 4, 9, 10, 11A, 11B, 25, 43, 48 and 53, Intellectual Property India website (consulted 14 November 2026); Gujarat Council on Science and Technology, Intellectual Property Facilitation Centre, formerly PIC, official GUJCOST website (consulted 14 November 2026); GUJCOST, IPFC Services, Patent Facilitation and IP Advisory sections (consulted 14 November 2026).]
